candidates.attacker_control: The entry names inside a scanned archive (zip/jar/war/ear/sar/apk/nupkg via ZipArchiveInputStream, and tar via TarArchiveInputStream; ArchiveAnalyzer lines 94 and 400-410) are fully attacker-controlled strings; dependency-check is designed to be pointed at untrusted third-party artifacts (CI builds, dependency trees, downloaded packages). analyzer.archive.enabled=true by default in core/src/main/resources/dependencycheck.properties (line 101), so the path runs on a default scan.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked for any containment validation in these paths: grep for getCanonicalPath/getCanonicalFile ('..', 'slip', 'traversal', 'outside') shows no check in ArchiveAnalyzer or ExtractionUtil (getCanonicalPath appears only in AbstractNpmAnalyzer, BaseDependencyCheckMojo and Settings). Checked whether engine.accept() blocks traversal entries: it only delegates to file-name/extension filters (SuffixFileFilter/NameFileFilter), so it constrains the *name* but not the *path*; an entry named '../../../../x.jar' is accepted. Checked whether the destination could be a non-temp path: ArchiveAnalyzer uses getSettings().getTempDirectory()+counter (lines 359-370) so '..' escapes it. Checked whether other extraction code is safe: JarAnalyzer.extractPom writes to a fixed 'pom.xml' name (lines 469-483) and AssemblyAnalyzer uses File.createTempFile (line 211), so they are not traversal sinks. Checked that ExtractionUtil's unfiltered overloads are currently unreferenced in-repo (only extractFilesUsingFilter is called, by PythonDistributionAnalyzer line 216), which weakens reachability of that copy but not of the ArchiveAnalyzer copy. Not verified at runtime: no execution, no malicious archive was built or run.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary file write outside the scanner's temporary extraction directory, with the privileges of the user running dependency-check. An attacker-supplied archive can create or overwrite files anywhere the process can write (limited to names matching an enabled analyzer's filter, e.g. *.jar/*.war/*.dll/*.exe/*.py). This allows tampering with the host/CI workspace and local caches, corrupting or replacing artifacts that are later loaded or executed by other tooling (e.g. dropping a JAR/DLL/EXE or overwriting a build/tool artifact), i.e. a realistic escalation path to code execution, and at minimum integrity loss and denial of service of the build machine.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The scanner processes an attacker-authored archive (the tool's normal use case). 2) The entry file name carries an extension/name accepted by some enabled FileTypeAnalyzer, because ArchiveAnalyzer only writes entries for which engine.accept(file) is true (line 522) — e.g. .jar/.war (JarAnalyzer EXTENSIONS), .dll/.exe (AssemblyAnalyzer), .py, .rb, plus name-based filters (METADATA/PKG-INFO in PythonDistributionAnalyzer). The match is done on the file name suffix only (FileFilterBuilder → SuffixFileFilter, FileFilterBuilder lines 132-134; Engine.accept lines 1012-1023), so a traversal path ending in an accepted name passes. 3) The resolved target location is writable by the scanning process (typical for developer machines and CI agents). For the ExtractionUtil filtered variant the only in-repo caller is PythonDistributionAnalyzer (line 216) with a name-only FILTER, so the file name must be METADATA or PKG-INFO; the unfiltered extractFiles(..) overloads currently have no caller inside the snapshot (they remain part of the public utils API).
candidates.root_cause: Archive entry names are used directly as relative paths with no normalization/containment check. In ArchiveAnalyzer.extractArchive a File is built as new File(destination, entry.getName()) (line 516) and handed to extractAcceptedFile, which creates parent directories and opens a FileOutputStream on that exact path (lines 542-547). ExtractionUtil does the same: new File(extractTo, entry.getName()) (line 102, written at line 104) and new File(destination, entry.getName()) (line 199, written at line 204). No code anywhere in these flows calls getCanonicalPath()/normalize() on the destination or the produced file, and no check exists for '..' or absolute entry names (searches for getCanonicalPath, getCanonicalFile, '..', 'slip', 'traversal', 'outside' return no such check in the extraction paths). Because the destination is only the analyzer's temporary directory (ArchiveAnalyzer.getNextTempDirectory, line 359-370, under Settings.getTempDirectory()), a crafted entry such as '../../../../<target>/x.jar' resolves outside it.
candidates.title: Unvalidated archive entry names in archive extraction (Zip Slip) allow files to be written outside the extraction directory
candidates.trace: ArchiveAnalyzer.analyzeDependency (line 231) → extractAndAnalyze (line 247) → extractFiles (line 380) → for known zip extensions: new ZipArchiveInputStream(in) then extractArchive(zin, destination, engine) (lines 405-406); for 'tar': TarArchiveInputStream then the same extractArchive (lines 409-410) → loop over input.getNextEntry() → new File(destination, entry.getName()) (line 516) → engine.accept(file) (line 522) → extractAcceptedFile(input, file) (line 540) → parent.mkdirs() (line 543) creates the '..'-based directory chain and new FileOutputStream(file) (line 547) writes attacker-controlled bytes to the resolved path. ExtractionUtil mirrors this: extractFiles (line 102-104, engine==null writes every entry), extractArchive → extractFile (line 199-204).
candidates.unverified: Runtime exploitability was not verified (no code/archives were executed). The exact set of target files an attacker can overwrite depends on enabled analyzers, their suffix filters and the writability of the resolved path; whether an overwritten artifact is later loaded/executed is deployment-specific. Behavior for absolute entry names differs by platform (File(parent, child) semantics), so the reliable vector is '..' sequences rather than absolute paths. Whether upstream Dependency-Check ever shipped a containment fix for these methods is outside the inspected snapshot and was not consulted.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal' / Zip Slip), leading to arbitrary file write

coverage_summary: Scope: get_source_scope reports 412 model-visible text files, 0 excluded by size (>5 MiB), 0 excluded by sensitive name/path, 0 symlinks; binary-like files are refused/skipped by the tools. get_relation_scope reports the index covers 393 of 412 files (209 Java files, all parsed; 1 parse error), 19 source files missing from the index, 8517 call sites with 6220 unresolved, and explicitly no control-flow, no data-flow and no semantic resolution — so all reachability/data-flow statements above come from reading source text, not from the index. I enumerated the whole tree and read all files relevant to attacker-controlled input: ArchiveAnalyzer, ExtractionUtil, JarAnalyzer extraction helpers, AssemblyAnalyzer, PythonDistributionAnalyzer, NodePackageAnalyzer/NspAnalyzer/ComposerLockParser (JSON), all XML parsers (XmlUtils, PomParser, HintParser, SuppressionParser, XPathNuspecParser, NvdCve handlers), CveDB/ConnectionFactory/dbStatements, Downloader/URLConnectionFactory/SSLSocketFactoryEx, ReportGenerator/EscapeTool, Engine, Settings, CLI/App/CliParser, Maven/Ant mojos and taskdefs, plus build/config files. Limitation: the snapshot contains main sources only — no src/test sources (0 test files) and non-text resources are absent (Velocity report templates *.vsl, XML schemas *.xsd, data/cwe.hashmap.serialized, GrokAssembly.exe), so report-template injection/escaping and the exact contents of those resources could not be reviewed; 19 files are unindexed and were not individually confirmed.
limitations: No code, tests, scanners or exploits were executed; findings are source-evidence only and are not runtime-confirmed.
The relation index has no control/data-flow or semantic resolution and 6220 unresolved calls, so the trace above is a manual source reading of the listed methods, not a proven data flow.
Test sources are absent from the snapshot, so intended-behavior/regression tests (e.g. for extraction safety) could not be consulted.

Non-text resources referenced by the code are missing from the snapshot (core/src/main/resources/templates/*.vsl, schema/*.xsd, data/cwe.hashmap.serialized, GrokAssembly.exe), so the HTML/report escaping path and the serialized CWE resource could not be inspected.

Whether upstream added a canonical-path/containment check in a later revision (i.e. whether this code is the pre-fix state of a known CVE) could not be verified from the snapshot alone; no external sources were consulted.

Exploitability depends on the set of enabled analyzers, their name/suffix filters, and writability of the resolved path in the target deployment; the file-name filter constraint and platform-specific handling of absolute entry names are the main mitigations observed.

rejected_leads.lead: Unsafe Java deserialization in core/src/main/java/org/owasp/dependencycheck/data/cwe/CweDB.java (loadData, lines 60-73) uses a plain ObjectInputStream to read the classpath resource 'data/cwe.hashmap.serialized', while the purpose-built filter class org.owasp.dependencycheck.utils.ExpectedObjectInputStream (lines 36-71) exists but is referenced nowhere in the snapshot (possible CWE-502 and a strong hint of a removed/absent hardening).
rejected_leads.reason: Attacker control is weak: the object comes from a resource bundled inside dependency-check's own jar/classpath, so exploitation would require the ability to place a malicious resource earlier on the tool's classloader (local/classpath influence that usually already implies code execution). It is a legitimate hardening gap but not the strongest attacker-controlled issue in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Path built from attacker-controlled keys in core/src/main/java/org/owasp/dependencycheck/analyzer/NodePackageAnalyzer.java (lines 219-247): name = package-lock.json dependency key, then Paths.get(baseDir, 'node_modules', name) and new File(base, 'package.json') are read into a Dependency if they exist.
rejected_leads.reason: Results only in reading a fixed-named file ('package.json') from a traversed directory; no write, no execution, and the found file only contributes 'evidence' to the report. Impact is too weak/uncertain to compete with the extraction issue.

rejected_leads.lead: NVD update path (DownloadTask/NvdCveUpdater/Downloader) downloads feeds without verifying a checksum or signature, so a MITM/proxy could tamper with the CVE data; SSLSocketFactoryEx defaults still include TLSv1/TLSv1.1 (utils/SSLSocketFactoryEx.java lines 265-271).
rejected_leads.reason: No integrity-check infrastructure exists anywhere in this revision (no SHA/signature verification code to compare against) and the protocol list is an explicit, configurable compatibility default (downloader.tls.protocols). These read as design/configuration posture rather than a concrete introduced flaw.

Counterevidence found: every parser uses XmlUtils.buildSecureSaxParser*/buildSecureDocumentBuilder (utils/…/XmlUtils.java lines 76-151) which sets disallow-doctype-decl=true and external-general-entities=false; the only relaxation is FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING left commented out for legacy suppression files, which does not re-enable entity resolution. Could not obtain a working XXE path.

All statements come from parameterized resource bundles (core/src/main/resources/data/dbStatements*.properties with '?' placeholders) and are executed as PreparedStatements; no attacker-controlled string concatenation into SQL was found.

summary: Repository is OWASP Dependency-Check (parent version 3.1.2, i.e. post-3.1.1 main sources) — a scanner whose primary input is untrusted third-party artifacts. I reviewed the extraction, XML parsing, database, download/TLS, reporting, process-execution and CLI paths in the text files present in the snapshot. Almost all classic sinks are already hardened at this revision (all XML parsers use XmlUtils with doctype/external-entity features disabled; all CveDB statements are prepared/parameterized; external processes are started with argument lists, not shells; SHA-1 inputs to Central/Nexus are regex-validated; temp files use File.createTempFile). The single strongest source-evidenced issue is the absence of any canonical/containment validation when archive entry names are turned into filesystem paths during extraction (Zip Slip / CWE-22), in the default-enabled ArchiveAnalyzer and in the shared ExtractionUtil. I could not verify exploitability at runtime (no execution permitted), and one plausible alternative (unsafe ObjectInputStream in CweDB) is recorded as a rejected lead.
